<reason>Both sides argued well and stayed within closed-book plausibility, but CON built the cleaner decision rule and defended it. CON's framing — long-run earnings equal gain per person times people reached, and apprenticeship reach is set by private firms rather than by appropriation — was established in the opening and never squarely neutralized. PRO's best answer ("it doesn't compel; it bribes away the bottleneck") conceded the mechanism CON needed, and CON exploited that quote in both later speeches; PRO's recession answer (hospitals, utilities, public construction) was fairly turned into an admission that the durable slots are already public. CON also landed the sharpest single catch of the debate: PRO's central villain is debt, but the motion compares subsidies, and grants are precisely the instrument that removes debt. PRO repeated the debt-compounding line in Rebuttal 2 and again in closing without ever engaging that distinction, leaving a live hole (PRO's foregone-earnings point is legitimate but was folded back into debt language). PRO scored real damage on completion versus enrollment ("seats respond to money only if you count bodies, not degrees") and gave a genuinely good answer to the selection pressure — "selection after tuition is crueler than selection before pay" — but CON's "every screen has a residual; the open door takes him" preserved the edge, and CON's underemployment response (mostly a first-job condition; graduates out-earn non-graduates in the same jobs) blunted PRO's slope-never-starts claim. CON's Rebuttal 2 was clipped for exceeding the limit, a real execution cost, but the lost material was weighing largely recovered in the closing. PRO's closing crystallized well but recycled the debt framing that CON had already disarmed, while CON's closing narrowed to the one word doing the work, "expanding," making the ballot easier.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's twin hits in Rebuttal 1: turning PRO's "apprentices produce while training" into evidence that money is not the binding constraint, and pointing out that PRO "keeps prosecuting loans in a debate about aid" since a subsidy is the instrument that removes debt. PRO never answered the second, and its own "bribes away the bottleneck" answer to CON's Q1 handed CON the scale framing that decided the round.</best_rebuttal>
